Work done equals the **change in kinetic energy**, so compare the two changes rather than
the two speeds.
**Step 1 — the work to go from v to 2v.**
W₁ = ½m(2v)² − ½mv²
= ½m(4v²) − ½mv²
= 2mv² − ½mv²
= **(3/2)mv²**
**Step 2 — the work to go from rest to v.**
W₂ = ½mv² − 0
= **½mv²**
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
W₁/W₂ = (3/2)mv² ÷ ½mv² = **3**
so the work is **three times** that needed to reach v from rest ✓
**Why it is not twice.** Kinetic energy goes as **v²**, not v ✓ Doubling the speed
**quadruples** the energy, from ½mv² to 2mv², and the extra required is the difference,
3 × ½mv² — three times the first stage, not one or two.
**A table of the energies.**
at rest: **0**
at v: **½mv²** — one unit
at 2v: **2mv²** — four units
at 3v: **4·5mv²** — nine units
Each stage costs more than the last: 1 unit, then **3**, then 5 ✓ the odd numbers, which
is the signature of a square law.
**A concrete instance.** A 1000 kg truck going from 10 to 20 m s⁻¹:
W₁ = ½(1000)(400 − 100) = **150 kJ**
and from rest to 10 m s⁻¹:
W₂ = ½(1000)(100) = **50 kJ** ✓ exactly three times.
**Reading the distractors.**
**four times** ✗ confuses the **final** kinetic energy (which is 4 times) with the
**work done in this stage** (which is the increase, 3 times) — the commonest error, and
the reason the option is offered.
**same as** ✗ would be true if energy went linearly with speed.
**less than** ✗ is the opposite of the truth: accelerating is **harder** at higher speed,
not easier.
**Why this matters in practice.** It is why overtaking at motorway speed needs far more
energy than pulling away from rest, and why braking distances grow as the square of
speed ✓
∴ three times as the work done in accelerating it from rest to v.

In **every** collision, elastic or not, the **total linear momentum** of the system is
conserved — provided no external force acts.
**Why momentum always survives.** By Newton's third law the two bodies exert equal and
opposite forces on each other, so the impulses they receive are equal and opposite:
Δp₁ = −Δp₂
and the total change is **zero** ✓ The internal forces cancel in pairs regardless of how
violent or lossy the collision is.
**Step — conclude.** The conserved quantity is the **total linear momentum** ✓
**Why kinetic energy is not conserved.** That is precisely what **inelastic** means ✗ Some
kinetic energy is converted into heat, sound and permanent deformation. In a **perfectly**
inelastic collision the bodies stick together and the loss is the greatest possible,
though never total — momentum conservation forbids both bodies ending at rest unless they
started with zero total momentum.
**A worked example.** A 2 kg body at 10 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary 3 kg body and they
stick together:
momentum before = 2(10) + 3(0) = **20 kg m s⁻¹**
common velocity after = 20/5 = **4 m s⁻¹**
momentum after = 5(4) = **20** ✓ conserved
KE before = ½(2)(100) = **100 J**
KE after = ½(5)(16) = **40 J** ✗ **60 J lost** to heat and deformation
**Why "speed of each body" is wrong.** The speeds change — that is what a collision does ✗
**Why "total mechanical energy" is wrong.** Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential.
The potential energy is unchanged in a collision on level ground, so this amounts to the
same claim as kinetic energy, and it fails for the same reason ✗ The lost energy has not
vanished — it has become **internal** energy, which mechanical energy does not count.
**The one proviso.** Momentum is conserved for the **system**, and only if the net
**external** force is zero or the collision is brief enough for external impulses to be
negligible ✓ In a collision the internal forces are enormous and the contact time tiny,
so this holds extremely well in practice.
∴ Total linear momentum.

On a **banked** road with friction, the maximum speed is reached when friction acts
**down** the slope at its limiting value.
**Step 1 — resolve the forces.** With the road banked at θ, a car of mass m at the point
of slipping outward has friction f = μN acting **down** the incline:
perpendicular to the road: **N = mg cos θ + (mv²/r) sin θ**
along the road: **(mv²/r) cos θ = mg sin θ + μN**
**Step 2 — eliminate N.** Substituting and collecting the v² terms:
(mv²/r)(cos θ − μ sin θ) = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ)
**Step 3 — solve for v².**
v² = rg(sin θ + μ cos θ)/(cos θ − μ sin θ)
**Step 4 — divide numerator and denominator by cos θ.**
v² = rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)
so
**v_max = √[rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]** ✓
**Check the special cases.**
**No friction** (μ = 0): v = √(rg tan θ) ✓ the familiar banking formula, where the speed
is fixed by the angle alone.
**No banking** (θ = 0): v = √(μrg) ✓ the maximum speed on a flat road, which is option
(c) — correct only in that special case, and offered as a trap.
**Both** (μ = 0 and θ = 0): v = 0 ✓ no turn is possible without either friction or
banking, as the formula says.
**Why the denominator has a minus.** As μ tan θ approaches 1 the denominator tends to
zero and v_max becomes **infinite** ✓ Physically, once the banking is steep enough the
road can hold the car at any speed — friction and the normal force together supply
whatever centripetal force is required.
**Why the numerator has a plus.** At maximum speed the car tends to slide **outward**, so
friction acts **inward and down** the slope, **adding** to the horizontal component of N ✓
Both effects push the same way, hence μ + tan θ.
**The companion result.** The **minimum** safe speed, below which the car slides inward,
reverses the friction and gives
v_min = √[rg(tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)]
— which is option (b) with its signs swapped ✓ Reading which extreme is wanted decides
between them.
∴ V = √[rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)].

On a **horizontal** road the entire centripetal force comes from friction, and the mass
cancels out.
**Step 1 — write the condition at the limiting speed.** The friction supplies the
centripetal force, and at the maximum it reaches μN with N = mg:
mv²/r = μmg
**Step 2 — cancel the mass.**
v²/r = μg
**v_max = √(μ r g)** ✓
**Step 3 — read off the dependence.** The safe speed depends on
**μ**, the coefficient of friction ✓ appears
**r**, the radius of the curve ✓ appears
**g**, the acceleration due to gravity ✓ appears
**m**, the mass — **cancels** ✗ does not appear
so the safe speed is **independent of the mass of the vehicle** ✓
**Why the mass cancels.** A heavier vehicle needs **more** centripetal force to turn —
but it also presses harder on the road, so friction supplies **proportionally more** ✓
Both sides of mv²/r = μmg scale with m, and the two effects balance exactly.
**A worked check.** With μ = 0·5, r = 50 m and g = 10 m s⁻²:
v_max = √(0·5 × 50 × 10) = √250 = **15·8 m s⁻¹ ≈ 57 km/h**
and the same figure applies to a motorcycle and to a loaded lorry ✓
**Why the other three do matter.**
**coefficient of friction** ✗ not independent — a wet road halves μ and cuts the safe
speed by √2, which is why cornering in rain is so much more dangerous.
**radius** ✗ not independent — a tighter bend has smaller r and a lower safe speed.
**g** ✗ not independent — on the Moon, with g six times smaller, the safe speed would be
√6 ≈ 2·4 times lower.
**The practical reading.** Mass independence is why speed limits on bends are posted as a
single number for all vehicles ✓ (In practice heavy vehicles are still more cautious,
because of their higher centre of mass and the risk of **toppling** rather than skidding —
a different failure mode, and one that does depend on the load.)
∴ Mass of vehicle.

Newton's second law relates the **magnitude** of the force to the mass and acceleration,
so find |F̄| first.
**Step 1 — compute the magnitude of the force.** With F̄ = 6î − 8ĵ + 10k̂:
|F̄| = √(6² + (−8)² + 10²)
= √(36 + 64 + 100)
= √200
= **10√2 N**
(since √200 = √(100 × 2) = 10√2 ≈ 14·14 N.)
**Step 2 — apply F = ma.**
m = |F̄|/a
= 10√2/1
= **10√2 kg** ✓
≈ **14·14 kg**.
**Why the magnitude and not the components.** The acceleration is given as a **scalar**,
1 m s⁻², meaning the magnitude of the acceleration vector. Since F̄ = mā with m a positive
scalar, the force and the acceleration are **parallel**, and their magnitudes satisfy
|F̄| = m|ā| ✓ So only the length of F̄ is needed.
**The direction, for completeness.** The acceleration points along
F̄/|F̄| = (6î − 8ĵ + 10k̂)/(10√2) = (0·424, −0·566, 0·707)
a unit vector ✓ and multiplying by 1 m s⁻² gives the acceleration vector itself.
**Checking the arithmetic.** 36 + 64 = 100, and 100 + 100 = **200** ✓ The two 100s —
one from 6² + 8² and one from 10² — are what make the answer a clean multiple of √2.
**Reading the distractors.**
**2√10 ≈ 6·32 kg** ✗ is √40, which would come from adding 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 and
mishandling, or from √(36 + 4). It is **smaller** than the largest single component of
the force divided by a, which is impossible: the magnitude of a vector is at least as
large as any one component, so m ≥ 10 kg ✓
**10 kg** ✗ uses only the k̂ component, ignoring the other two.
**20 kg** ✗ would need |F̄| = 20, but 20² = 400 ≠ 200.
That lower bound — **m ≥ 10** — eliminates option (b) at a glance, and the exact sum 200
settles the rest ✓
**A caution.** |F̄| is **not** 6 + 8 + 10 = 24. Vector magnitudes add in quadrature, not
linearly ✓ (24 kg is not offered, but the error is common enough to be worth naming.)
∴ 10√2 kg.

The ball **reverses** direction, so its momentum changes by **twice** mv — the single
point on which this question turns.
**Step 1 — convert to SI units.**
m = 10 g = **0·01 kg**
**Step 2 — set up a sign convention.** Take downward (towards the surface) as positive:
initial velocity **u = +5 m s⁻¹**
final velocity **v = −5 m s⁻¹** (rebounding upward at the same speed)
**Step 3 — find the change in momentum.**
Δp = m(v − u)
= 0·01(−5 − 5)
= 0·01(−10)
= **−0·1 kg m s⁻¹**
of magnitude **0·1 N s**, directed upward ✓
**Step 4 — apply the impulse-momentum theorem.**
F = Δp/Δt
= 0·1/0·01
= **10 N** ✓
**Why the factor of two matters.** Had the ball simply **stopped** on impact, the change
would be only 0·01 × 5 = 0·05 kg m s⁻¹ and the force would be **5 N** ✓ Because it
rebounds at the same speed, the momentum swings from +0·05 to −0·05 — a total change of
**0·1** ✓ Reversal costs twice as much as stopping.
**The direction of the force.** The ball's momentum changes **upward**, so the surface
pushes the ball **upward** with 10 N ✓ and by Newton's third law the ball pushes down on
the surface with 10 N.
**A check on the size.** The ball's weight is only
mg = 0·01 × 9·8 = **0·098 N**
so the impact force is about **100 times** the weight ✓ which is why the weight can be
ignored during so brief a contact, and why collisions feel so much sharper than steady
loads.
**Reading the distractors.**
**100 N** ✗ is ten times too large — it comes from using 10 g as 0·1 kg, a factor-of-ten
slip in the unit conversion.
**1 N** ✗ and **0·1 N** ✗ are ten and a hundred times too small; 0·1 is the **impulse**
in N s, not the force, and mistaking one for the other is the other common error ✓
**The two quantities to keep apart.** Impulse **J = Δp = 0·1 N s** (a momentum), and
average force **F = J/Δt = 10 N**. Dividing by the contact time is the final step, and
0·01 s is a small divisor, which is exactly why the force comes out large ✓
∴ 10 N.

In uniform circular motion the **speed** is constant but the **direction** of every vector
quantity keeps turning — so only a quantity built from speed alone survives.
**Testing each option.**
**Velocity** ✗ — velocity is a **vector**. Its magnitude is constant but its direction
changes continuously as the body goes round, so the velocity itself is **not** constant ✓
(This is the whole reason the motion is accelerated.)
**Acceleration** ✗ — the centripetal acceleration has constant magnitude **v²/r** but
always points **towards the centre**, so its direction turns with the body ✗ not constant.
**Centripetal force** ✗ — same objection: **mv²/r** in magnitude, but a continuously
changing direction ✗
**Kinetic energy** ✓ — **½mv²** is a **scalar** built only from the **speed**, which is
given as constant. It has no direction to change, so it stays fixed ✓
**Step — conclude.** The kinetic energy remains constant ✓
**Why the kinetic energy must be constant.** The centripetal force is always
**perpendicular** to the velocity, so it does **no work**:
W = F̄ · d̄ = Fd cos 90° = **0**
and by the work-energy theorem the kinetic energy cannot change ✓ The force changes the
direction of motion without ever speeding the body up or slowing it down.
**A concrete illustration.** A 2 kg mass circling at 3 m s⁻¹ on a 1·5 m string:
speed **3 m s⁻¹** — constant ✓
kinetic energy ½(2)(9) = **9 J** — constant ✓
acceleration v²/r = 9/1·5 = **6 m s⁻²** — constant in size, but pointing north, then
east, then south, then west as the mass goes round ✗
velocity — **3 m s⁻¹** east, then south, then west ✗
**The distinction the question tests.** "Constant" for a **vector** demands both
magnitude **and** direction; for a **scalar** only the one number. Three of the four
options are vectors and all three fail on direction; the only scalar is the answer ✓
**A related point.** The **magnitude** of the acceleration is constant, and a careless
reading of option (b) as "the magnitude of the acceleration" would make it true. But
acceleration is a vector, and the question asks what **remains constant** — so the
vector's turning disqualifies it ✓
∴ Kinetic energy.
